analysis.one_liner: Lets FDA investigators sample large animal farms during foodborne illness outbreaks.
analysis.headline: A bill giving the FDA power to sample large livestock farms during food poisoning outbreaks was introduced in February 2025 with two sponsors and has not moved since it reached the Senate health committee.
analysis.plain_summary: When people get sick from contaminated food, investigators often can't trace the source to the farm. This bill would let the Food and Drug Administration request access to large confined animal operations — feedlots, dairies, and poultry farms big enough to be regulated as CAFOs — to take samples of animals, plants, water, and the environment during an outbreak investigation. Farms that refuse could be penalized, and the data would be shared with USDA and state health agencies. The bill went to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced and has had no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who would get faster answers about what made them sick and where contaminated food came from; and public health agencies, which would get the on-farm evidence they currently lack when tracing outbreaks. State and federal health departments also gain access to shared data.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who eat meat, dairy, and produce

how_it_helps.text: The FDA can request access to a large confined animal operation to conduct microbial sampling when it determines sampling is needed for a foodborne-illness outbreak investigation, to find an outbreak's root cause, or to address other public health needs.

Operations that receive a request must provide reasonable access, including sampling of plants, animals, water, and the environment, though farms may set reasonable conditions on time, place, and manner.
Refusing to provide reasonable access would become a prohibited act under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, giving the FDA an enforcement tool against farms that block investigators.
Sampling data must be shared with the Secretary of Agriculture and relevant state and federal public health agencies to help detect, investigate, and prevent foodborne illness.

analysis.who_pays: Large concentrated animal feeding operations — big feedlots, dairy operations, and poultry farms — which would have to open their property to federal samplers during investigations and could face penalties for refusing. Smaller farms fall below the CAFO size threshold and are not covered.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large confined livestock and poultry operations

drawbacks.text: The bill puts a new government entry-and-inspection obligation on farms: an operation that receives a request must allow sampling of animals, plants, water, and its environment, and can be charged with a prohibited act for refusing. Farm groups and owners have long resisted on-farm federal access on biosecurity and property-rights grounds.

The obligation falls only on operations large enough to be defined as concentrated animal feeding operations under the EPA's regulations, so the burden is targeted at the biggest farms rather than spread evenly across agriculture.
The bill does not add any new inspection requirements for foods under USDA jurisdiction beyond microbial sampling, which limits how much of the meat supply chain it actually covers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the public, the upside is concrete: faster identification of what farm or contamination source caused an outbreak, which can end recalls sooner and prevent more illnesses. The cost falls on a narrow set of large livestock operations that must accommodate investigators, and farms retain the ability to set reasonable conditions on when and how sampling happens. The main weakness is that the bill covers only FDA sampling authority and leaves USDA-regulated inspection largely untouched, so it is a targeted fix rather than a sweeping overhaul of meat safety.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate health committee on February 3, 2025, and has sat there without a hearing, a committee vote, or any floor action since.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the bill on February 3, 2025, joined by Senator Richard Blumenthal as cosponsor.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed: large confined animal operations continue to operate without any federal obligation to allow on-farm microbial sampling during outbreak investigations, and FDA investigators still lack this access tool. Consumers have gained nothing yet because the bill has not advanced.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded its referral to the HELP Committee.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: Both supporters are Democrats, and no opposition appears anywhere in the record; no Republican has cosponsored or spoken against it, and the committee has simply not acted.

industries.industry: Concentrated animal feeding operations (large feedlots, dairies, and poultry farms)
industries.note: The bill would require these operations to admit FDA samplers during outbreak investigations and makes refusal a punishable violation, adding an oversight burden that does not exist today. Their interest in staying closed to investigators runs against the public's interest in tracing contaminated food to its source.
Faster identification of outbreak sources could narrow recalls and reduce the scope and duration of recalls that disrupt food suppliers and shake consumer confidence.

analysis.trajectory: Bills with a single cosponsor that sit in committee without a hearing rarely reach the floor. Unless the HELP Committee schedules a markup or a broader food-safety package picks up this provision, S. 376 will likely remain dormant for the rest of the 119th Congress.
